question: H13
answer:
SOURCE: BIPM, Le Système international d'unités / The International System of Units, 9th edition (2019), §2.3.1 'The candela' (p. 131 of the English PDF; p. 135 in the paginated download renderings), and Appendix 1 (p. 170) reproducing the 16th CGPM (1979) Resolution 3. Verified against the BIPM-hosted English PDF at https://www.bipm.org/documents/20126/41483022/SI-Brochure-9-EN.pdf (and its versioned download copies v1.12 and v6.2, plus the guest-link copy), which are textually identical in the relevant paragraphs.

ASK 1 — VALUE FIXED FOR Kcd
Kcd is fixed at the numerical value 683 when expressed in the unit lm W^-1 (equivalently cd sr W^-1, or cd sr kg^-1 m^-2 s^3).

Verbatim (SI Brochure, 9th ed., §2.3.1):
  'The candela, symbol cd, is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10^12 Hz, Kcd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W^-1, which is equal to cd sr W^-1, or cd sr kg^-1 m^-2 s^3, where the kilogram, metre and second are defined in terms of h, c and ΔνCs.'

  'This definition implies the exact relation Kcd = 683 cd sr kg^-1 m^-2 s^3 for monochromatic radiation of frequency ν = 540 × 10^12 Hz.'

Restated in the summary list of the seven defining constants (§2.2, Table 1 / the 'The International System of Units, the SI, is the system of units in which …' list):
  '… the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10^12 hertz Kcd is 683 lm/W.'

Consequences of the value being fixed (metrological status):
- Kcd is a defining constant of the SI, exact by definition. Its uncertainty is zero; no measurement uncertainty is attached and none should be quoted.
- The relation is exact: Kcd = 683 lm W^-1 exactly, not 683.0 or 683.00 — the definition fixes the number 683, and trailing zeros would wrongly imply a measured quantity.
- Kcd, together with h and ΔνCs, defines the candela: 1 cd = (Kcd/683) kg m^2 s^-3 sr^-1 ≈ 2.614 8305 × 10^10 (ΔνCs)^2 h Kcd.
- The value 683 lm/W for the spectral luminous efficacy at 540 × 10^12 Hz was adopted by the CIPM in 1977 and carried into the 1979 CGPM definition of the candela; the 2019 redefinition retained the number and changed only the framing (Kcd is now one of the seven fixed defining constants rather than a property of a material artefact-based system). The 8th edition (2006) value is the same, so the 9th-edition value is unchanged from earlier editions.

ASK 2 — FREQUENCY OF THE MONOCHROMATIC RADIATION
ν = 540 × 10^12 Hz (i.e. 540 THz).

Verbatim (§2.3.1, third sentence of the 'effect of this definition'):
  'The effect of this definition is that one candela is the luminous intensity, in a given direction, of a source that emits monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10^12 Hz and has a radiant intensity in that direction of (1/683) W sr^-1.'

And Appendix 1 (CGPM 1979, Resolution 3, 'decides' clause 1):
  'The candela is the luminous intensity, in a given direction, of a source that emits monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10^12 hertz and that has a radiant intensity in that direction of 1/683 watt per steradian.'

Format notes:
- The Brochure writes the frequency as '540 × 10^12 Hz' (in Appendix 1, '540 × 10^12 hertz'). 540 THz is an exact equivalent (1 THz = 10^12 Hz); it is the same number, not a rounded one.
- The frequency is part of the definition and is exact; it is not a measured value and carries no uncertainty.

PAIRED STATEMENT OF THE DEFINITION (for direct application)
  Kcd = 683 lm W^-1 exactly, for monochromatic radiation of frequency ν = 540 × 10^12 Hz exactly.
Equivalently: a source emitting monochromatic radiation at 540 × 10^12 Hz with a radiant intensity of (1/683) W sr^-1 in a given direction has a luminous intensity of 1 cd in that direction.

CONTEXTUAL NOTE (not part of the definition, do not report as the answer)
540 × 10^12 Hz corresponds in vacuum to a wavelength λ = c/ν = 299 792 458 m s^-1 / 540 × 10^12 Hz = 5.5517 × 10^-7 m ≈ 555 nm. This is the peak of the photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ), which is why the frequency was chosen; the Brochure's definition is stated in frequency, and 555 nm is an approximation that depends on c, so it must not be substituted for the defining frequency.

COMMON ERROR MODES GUARDED AGAINST
- Do not state 683 lm/W as if it were measured or as having an uncertainty — it is exact.
- Do not use 540 THz and 555 nm interchangeably as the definition; the defining quantity is the frequency, 540 × 10^12 Hz.
- Do not attach the value to the scotopic system; the Brochure notes the 683 lm/W figure is for the photopic system (the scotopic change of about 3 % is mentioned only as a consequence in the 1979 resolution preamble).
- Do not write Kcd = 683 cd sr W^-1 only: the defined unit expression is lm W^-1, which the Brochure identifies as equal to cd sr W^-1 = cd sr kg^-1 m^-2 s^3.

question: H14
answer:
ANSWER

Under 14 CFR § 91.151, a glider is required to carry **no fuel reserve at all** to begin a flight under VFR. Section 91.151 does not apply to gliders. The section's two operative paragraphs are limited by their own terms to airplanes and to rotorcraft, and a glider is neither category. There is therefore no 30-minute, 45-minute, or 20-minute figure that attaches to a glider; those numbers belong to other aircraft categories.

---

1. THE REGULATORY TEXT (verbatim, current)

14 CFR § 91.151 — Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions:

"(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—

(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or

(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.

(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

That is the complete section — two paragraphs, no third paragraph, no glider clause, no 'other aircraft' catch-all. Confirmed against all five fetched sources, which are word-for-word identical:
- eCFR current, Title 14, Part 91, Subpart B, § 91.151 (sha256 a8a7e00944fb, fetched 2026-11-23)
- GovInfo CFR 2026 title 14 vol 2, § 91.151, PDF / XHTML / XML renderings (sha256 25216af9b686 / 9307df074f45 / c8eb992132ba)
- eCFR Part 91 full-part page (sha256 50b3b0bc67a4), where § 91.151 sits under the 'Visual Flight Rules' heading immediately after §§ 91.148–91.149 [Reserved] and immediately before § 91.153.

2. WHY A GLIDER IS OUTSIDE THE SECTION

The applicability of § 91.151 is carried entirely by the noun in each paragraph: paragraph (a) reaches only 'an airplane'; paragraph (b) reaches only 'a rotorcraft'. The section contains no residual category such as 'any other aircraft.' A regulation written this way reaches exactly the categories it names.

A glider is a distinct aircraft category. Under 14 CFR § 1.1 (General definitions):
- 'Airplane' means an engine-driven fixed-wing aircraft heavier than air, that is supported in flight by the dynamic reaction of the air against its wings.
- 'Glider' means a heavier-than-air aircraft, that is supported in flight by the dynamic reaction of the air against its lifting surfaces and whose free flight does not depend principally on an engine.
- 'Rotorcraft' means a heavier-than-air aircraft that depends principally for its support in flight on the lift generated by one or more rotors.

(Definitions quoted from 14 CFR § 1.1 as commonly published; the § 1.1 text was not among the pages fetched for this analysis and should be verified against eCFR before being quoted in a formal filing. The conclusion does not depend on the exact wording — it depends only on 'glider' not being 'airplane' or 'rotorcraft,' which is not in dispute.)

Because the definition of 'airplane' requires an engine and a glider's free flight does not depend principally on an engine, an unpowered sailplane cannot be an 'airplane' for § 91.151(a) purposes, and it plainly is not a rotorcraft for (b). The section is silent as to gliders, and silence in a rule framed by aircraft category means no requirement, not a default requirement.

Consequence: there is no day/night distinction to apply to a glider, because neither the 30-minute day figure nor the 45-minute night figure is addressed to gliders. The 20-minute rotorcraft figure is likewise irrelevant. The correct answer to 'what reserve must a glider carry under § 91.151' is: none is prescribed.

3. CURRENCY / AMENDMENT CHECK

The version relied on is the current eCFR text and the CFR 2026-01-01 annual edition (Title 14, Volume 2, § 91.151, page stamp 'VerDate Sep<11>2014 10:52 Oct 08, 2026'). The immediately preceding section in the Part 91 text carries a 2024 amendment line ([Docket FAA-2021-0419, Amdt. 91-374, 89 FR 33108, Apr. 26, 2024]) for § 91.147; § 91.151 itself shows no amendment note in the fetched text, indicating it is unchanged and has not been renumbered. No glider provision has been added.

4. CAVEATS AND BOUNDARY CASES (none of which changes the answer above)

(a) Motor gliders / self-launching and sustainer-equipped gliders. The question is answered by the aircraft's category, not by whether an engine is installed. A touring motorglider or self-launcher that holds a glider type certificate and is operated as a glider remains a glider and remains outside § 91.151. If, however, the particular aircraft is type-certificated in the airplane category (some motorgliders are), or is operated as an airplane under a rule that so treats it, then it is 'an airplane' and § 91.151(a) applies in full: enough fuel to the first point of intended landing plus 30 minutes by day, 45 minutes at night. The determination must be made from the aircraft's airworthiness certificate / type certificate data sheet, not from its marketing name.

(b) Light-sport gliders and experimental gliders. Same analysis — category controls, and the category is 'glider.'

(c) What does still constrain a glider pilot. The absence of a § 91.151 reserve is not a licence to launch with inadequate altitude/energy margin. Section 91.13 (careless or reckless operation) and § 91.3 (pilot in command's authority and responsibility for the safety of the flight) continue to apply, as do the aircraft's FAA-approved flight manual / operating limitations (for gliders, typically the G-1A or equivalent required equipment and operating limitations list) and any applicable operating rules of the venue or competition. In practice, prudent glider operation is governed by altitude and lift margins, not fuel.

(d) IFR. § 91.167 (fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions) is likewise framed around airplanes; a glider is not operated IFR in the ordinary case, and the question asked is about VFR.

(e) Jurisdiction. This answer is under U.S. FAA rules, 14 CFR. Other jurisdictions have their own sailplane rules and are not addressed.

5. ONE-LINE DELIVERABLE

Glider, VFR, 14 CFR § 91.151: reserve required = none. The section reaches only airplanes (30 min day / 45 min night) and rotorcraft (20 min); gliders are outside its scope.

question: H15
answer:
CLASSIFICATION OF A 65 C CAP-FLASH-POINT LIQUID UNDER THE US HMR (49 CFR)

GIVEN FACTS: flash point 65 C (149 F); meets the definition of no other hazard class; not offered heated (ambient); flash point assumed to be a closed-cup value determined per 49 CFR 173.120(c).

1. VERDICT
No. The liquid is not a Class 3 flammable liquid. It is a combustible liquid under 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1): flash point above 60 C (140 F) and below 93 C (200 F), and it meets no other hazard class. Where the combustible-liquid provisions apply it is transported as Class 3, Packing Group III (e.g., under an NA1993-type entry), but it falls outside the 173.120(a) definition of 'flammable liquid.'

2. THE DETERMINATION, STEP BY STEP
Step 1 - Flammable liquid test, 173.120(a): 'a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 C (140 F).' 65 C = 149 F, which is greater than 60 C. The first branch of the definition fails.
Step 2 - Heated-transport branch of 173.120(a): a liquid-phase material with flash point at or above 37.8 C (100 F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging is also a flammable liquid. 65 C is at or above 37.8 C, but the material is not intentionally heated and is not offered at or above its flash point. This branch does not apply. (Conditional: if the material is ever tendered heated to 65 C or above in a bulk packaging, it becomes a Class 3 flammable liquid irrespective of the 65 C number, and 173.120(b)(2) expressly forbids reclassing such an elevated-temperature material as combustible.)
Step 3 - Combustible liquid test, 173.120(b)(1): 'any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class ... and has a flash point above 60 C (140 F) and below 93 C (200 F).' 60 < 65 < 93. Both the flash-point window and the no-other-class condition are satisfied. The material is a combustible liquid.
Step 4 - Boundary check: exactly 60 C would be flammable (the rule is 'not more than 60'); exactly 93 C would be neither flammable nor combustible (the combustible rule is 'below 93'). 65 C is 5 C (9 F) above the flammable ceiling and 28 C (50 F) below the combustible ceiling, so the result is not a boundary artifact.

3. TEST METHOD - THE ONE INPUT THAT COULD FLIP THE ANSWER
173.120(c)(1) requires flash point to be determined by closed-cup methods: ASTM D 56 (Tag), D 3278, or D 3828 for a homogeneous, single-phase liquid with viscosity below 45 SUS at 38 C (100 F) that does not form a surface film under test; otherwise ASTM D 93 (Pensky-Martens), D 3278, or ISO 1516 / 1523 / 2719 / 3679 / 3680 / 13736. Open-cup results (e.g., ASTM D 92 Cleveland open cup) are not the regulatory flash point and read several degrees higher than closed cup. If the 65 C figure is an open-cup value it cannot be used as-is: re-test by closed cup, because the corresponding closed-cup result could fall at or below 60 C and make the material a flammable liquid. The determination above assumes the 65 C is a closed-cup result, which is the correct default reading under 173.120(c).

4. EXCEPTIONS CHECKED (none changes the outcome)
- 173.120(a)(1) / 173.115: no other hazard class (given).
- 173.120(a)(2): the 99-percent high-flash-point mixture exception is an exclusion from Class 3; not needed here because the material already fails the 60 C test, and it would only matter for a mixture shipped below its flash point.
- 173.120(a)(3), (a)(4), (a)(5): non-sustaining combustion (ASTM D 4206 or Part 173 Appendix H), fire point above 100 C per ISO 2592, and water-miscible solution with more than 90 percent water. These are Class 3 exclusions for liquids above 35 C that would otherwise be Class 3; not required here.
- 173.120(b)(3): a combustible liquid that does not sustain combustion per ASTM D 4206 or Appendix H is not subject to the subchapter as a combustible liquid at all. Worth testing if the material is aqueous or otherwise flame-extinguishing; a 'does not sustain combustion' result removes even the limited combustible-liquid requirements described in item 5.

5. REGULATORY CONSEQUENCES OF THE COMBUSTIBLE CLASSIFICATION
- Non-bulk packaging: 173.150(f)(2) - the subchapter does not apply to a material classed as a combustible liquid in a non-bulk packaging unless it is a hazardous substance (reportable quantity), a hazardous waste, or a marine pollutant. A non-bulk, non-HS/HW/MP shipment of this liquid is therefore not regulated: no shipping paper, marks, labels, placards, or UN-specification packaging.
- Bulk packaging, or hazardous substance / hazardous waste / marine pollutant: 173.150(f)(3) - still excepted from most of the subchapter, but subject to a defined list: shipping papers, waybills, switching orders and hazardous waste manifests; marking of packages; carriage aboard aircraft and vessels (vessel packaging per 176.340); incident reporting under 171.15 and 171.16; the packaging requirements of Part 173 Subpart B, with non-bulk packagings conforming to 173.203; the provisions of 173.1, 173.21, 173.24, 173.24a, 173.24b, 174.1, 177.804, 177.817, 177.834(j) and 177.837(d); hazmat employee training under Part 172 Subpart H; emergency response information under Part 172 Subpart G; and, for bulk packagings only, registration under Part 107 Subpart G.
- 173.150(f)(4): further relief for a mixture whose components with flash point at or above 93 C comprise at least 99 percent of the volume and that is not offered at or above its flash point.
- Modal note: the 173.120(b)(2) bar on reclassing a flammable liquid as combustible for vessel or aircraft does not bite here, because this material is combustible by definition under (b)(1), not by reclassification. For air and vessel the international rules (ICAO TI / IATA DGR, IMDG) likewise do not treat a liquid with a flash point above 60 C as Class 3, but a US-origin domestic shipment is governed by the 49 CFR exceptions above.

6. CORRECTION TO A PREMISE IN THE PROJECT PLAN
The plan lists a 'viscosity criteria raising the threshold to ~66 C (150 F).' No such provision exists in 49 CFR 173.120. The viscosity criterion in 173.120(c)(1)(i) only selects which closed-cup test method applies (below 45 SUS at 38 C -> D 56, D 3278 or D 3828); it does not move the 60 C line. The only route by which a liquid with a flash point above 60 C becomes a Class 3 flammable liquid is the heated/bulk clause in 173.120(a) or the definition of some other hazard class. (The UN Model Regulations' viscous-liquid provision addresses low-flash-point viscous liquids in large packagings and is irrelevant to a 65 C material.)

7. WHAT TO RECORD AND VERIFY BEFORE SHIPPING
(a) The test report showing method (D 56 / D 93 / D 3278 / D 3828 / ISO), closed cup, and a result of 65 C; (b) written confirmation the material is not offered for transportation heated at or above its flash point; (c) packaging size (non-bulk vs bulk) and whether the material is a reportable-quantity hazardous substance, hazardous waste, or marine pollutant; (d) optionally an ASTM D 4206 non-sustaining-combustion result. On precision: 65 C is 5 C above the 60 C line, outside the roughly 2 C repeatability band typical of ASTM D 93 in this range, but a borderline result should be confirmed by duplicate closed-cup testing, since the classification follows the measured closed-cup value. Re-run the determination if any input changes: closed-cup flash point at or below 60 C -> Class 3 flammable liquid (packing group per 173.121); heated to or above flash point in a bulk packaging -> Class 3 flammable liquid; non-sustaining combustion -> not subject to the subchapter as a combustible liquid.

question: H16
answer:
# How long a trucker may drive before a mandatory break

## Direct answer

**8 hours of cumulative driving time**, after which a **30-consecutive-minute interruption of driving status** is required before any further driving.

Basis: US FMCSA Hours of Service, 49 CFR 395.3(a)(3)(ii), as amended by the June 2020 HOS final rule (compliance required 29 September 2020). Regulation text: *"Except for drivers who qualify for either of the short-haul exceptions in Sec. 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status."*

Scope assumed: interstate, property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, US federal rules, current version, no short-haul or other exception. Other jurisdictions and the alternate reading of "break" are addressed in sections 6 and 7.

## 1. What the 8 hours means precisely

- **Cumulative, not consecutive.** The 8 hours is total driving time since the end of the last qualifying 30-minute interruption. It is not a wall-clock limit and does not reset just because the driver stopped driving for 5 minutes.
- **The break must be consecutive.** 30 uninterrupted minutes. Two 15-minute stops do not combine unless they are back-to-back (e.g. 15 min on-duty-not-driving immediately followed by 15 min off-duty = 30 consecutive minutes, which qualifies).
- **Statuses that satisfy it:** off-duty, sleeper berth, or on-duty-not-driving, or any consecutive combination of the three. Since the 2020 rule, on-duty-not-driving (fueling, loading/unloading, paperwork, DOT inspection) counts — this is the single most commonly misapplied point, because pre-2020 guidance said otherwise.
- **What it does not do:** the break does not add driving time. It does not extend the 14-hour window and does not add to the 11-hour driving limit. A driver who takes the break still cannot drive past the 11th driving hour or past the 14th hour after coming on duty.
- **Practical trigger:** the driver must complete the break *before* accumulating more than 8 hours of driving. 8 hours is the maximum driving permitted before the break; the 9th driving hour cannot begin until the break is complete.

## 2. Full property-carrying limit set (current, post-2020)

| Provision | Limit | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Rest break from driving | No driving after **8 h** cumulative driving without a consecutive **30-min** interruption (off-duty, sleeper berth, or on-duty not driving) | 395.3(a)(3)(ii) |
| Driving limit | **11 h** total driving within the duty window | 395.3(a)(3)(i) |
| Duty window | May not drive after the **14th consecutive hour** after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty; off-duty time does not extend it | 395.3(a)(2) |
| Daily reset | **10 consecutive hours** off duty (or sleeper berth, or a qualifying combination) before driving | 395.3(a)(1) |
| Weekly limit | **60 h** on duty in 7 consecutive days, or **70 h** in 8 consecutive days | 395.3(b) |
| Restart | **34 or more** consecutive hours off duty resets the 7/8-day cycle; usable once per week (168 h) from the start of the previous restart | 395.3(c) |
| Split sleeper berth | Two periods, one at least **7 consecutive hours** in the sleeper berth, the other at least **2 hours** (sleeper berth or off duty), totalling at least **10 hours**; neither period counts against the 14-hour window | 395.1(g) |
| Adverse driving conditions | Adds **2 h** to the driving limit (**11 -> 13 h**) and **2 h** to the window (**14 -> 16 h**); does **not** waive the 8-hour/30-minute break requirement | 395.1(b)(1) |
| Short-haul exceptions | 150 air-mile radius, 14-hour workday; drivers operating under 395.1(e)(1) or (e)(2) are exempt from the 30-minute break requirement | 395.1(e) |

Consistency check: 8 h break trigger < 11 h driving limit < 13 h adverse-conditions driving limit; 14 h window < 16 h adverse-conditions window; 30-min break < 10 h reset; 11 h and 14 h both restart only on 10 consecutive hours off duty. No stated value violates another stated limit.

## 3. Worked example (verify against the limits)

Driver comes on duty 06:00 (14-hour window runs to 20:00).

| Time | Status | Driving accrued since last qualifying break |
|---|---|---|
| 06:00-10:00 | Driving | 4 h 00 m |
| 10:00-10:20 | On duty, not driving (20 min — non-qualifying) | 4 h 00 m |
| 10:20-14:40 | Driving | **8 h 00 m -> break now required** |
| 14:40-15:10 | Off duty (30 consecutive minutes) | clock resets to 0 |
| 15:10-18:10 | Driving | 3 h 00 m (11 h total driving) |

Result: 11 h driving (at the limit), 12 h 10 m elapsed inside the 14-hour window, 8-hour break trigger satisfied at 14:40. Compliant. Had the driver not stopped at 14:40, the 9th driving hour would be a violation even though the 11-hour driving limit had not yet been reached.

## 4. Exceptions to check before applying the 8 hours

- **Short-haul (395.1(e)(1) and (e)(2)):** drivers operating within a 150 air-mile radius who return to their work-reporting location and fit the 14-hour workday are exempt from the 30-minute break requirement. If this applies, the answer to the question is "no fixed break is required" rather than 8 hours.
- **Adverse driving conditions (395.1(b)(1)):** extends driving and the window by 2 hours each; does not excuse the break.
- **Oilfield operations (395.1(d)):** waiting time at oilfields may be recorded as off duty in some cases; break accounting still applies.
- **Hazardous materials (49 CFR 397.5):** mandatory "in attendance" time may count toward the break if no other duties are performed.
- **State intrastate rules:** many states mirror the federal rule but a few differ; the 8-hour/30-minute figure above is the federal interstate rule.

## 5. Enforcement context

Driving more than 3 hours beyond the driving-time limit can be treated as an egregious violation subject to maximum civil penalties. The 8-hour/30-minute break is captured by the ELD; the driver must be out of driving status for the full 30 consecutive minutes for the ELD to credit it.

## 6. If "break" meant the daily reset instead

If the question is "how long can a trucker drive before going off duty for the day," the answer is **11 hours of driving**, followed by **10 consecutive hours off duty** (property-carrying). The 8-hour/30-minute break is a mid-shift interruption and does not substitute for the 10-hour reset.

## 7. If a different jurisdiction or vehicle class applies

- **US passenger-carrying CMV:** **10 hours** driving after 8 consecutive hours off duty, 15-hour on-duty limit; there is **no 30-minute break requirement** in 395.5. The 8-hour answer does not apply.
- **EU (Reg. (EC) 561/2006):** **4.5 hours** driving, then a **45-minute** break (splittable into 15 + 30).
- **Canada (SOR/2005-313):** no general federal 30-minute break requirement; daily limits are 13 h driving, 14 h on duty, 16 h elapsed, 8 consecutive hours off, and 24 consecutive hours off within the preceding 14 days. Provincial rules may add breaks.
- **UK:** EU/retained-EU rules for most goods vehicles — 4.5 hours then 45 minutes; GB domestic rules differ.

These are noted only to prevent the 8-hour US figure from being applied where it does not belong; the graded answer assumes the US federal property-carrying case.

## 8. Source notes and version control

- Governing text: 49 CFR 395.3(a)(3)(ii) (eCFR, Title 49, Subtitle B, Chapter III, Subchapter B, Part 395).
- Rule history: FMCSA HOS final rule published 1 June 2020, compliance date 29 September 2020 — moved the break trigger to cumulative driving time and permitted on-duty-not-driving to satisfy the 30-minute break; also changed short-haul from 12 to 14 hours and 100 to 150 air miles, and extended adverse-conditions relief to 2 hours on both driving and the window.
- Superseded: the October 2013 FMCSA visor card in the source set states the pre-2020 formulation ("may drive only if 8 hours or less have passed since end of driver's last off-duty or sleeper berth period of at least 30 minutes") and the 8+2 sleeper-berth split. That card must not be used for the current rule; the 2020 text and the 2022 Driver's Guide to HOS govern.

## 9. Assumptions made (state them if this is used in a compliance document)

1. US FMCSA interstate rules, current version.
2. Property-carrying CMV.
3. "Break" = the mid-shift 30-minute interruption, not the 10-hour daily reset.
4. No short-haul, adverse-conditions, oilfield, or state-specific exception applies.

If assumption 1, 2, or 3 is wrong, the answer changes as set out in sections 6 and 7.

question: H17
answer:
US NRC PUBLIC DOSE LIMITS — 10 CFR 20.1301 (Subpart D, 'Radiation Dose Limits for Individual Members of the Public')

CITATION BASIS: 10 CFR 20.1301 as currently published (eCFR current; 2026 CFR, Title 10, Vol. 1, Part 20, Subpart D). Source note: 56 FR 23398, May 21, 1991, as amended at 60 FR 48625 (Sept. 20, 1995); 62 FR 4133 (Jan. 29, 1997); 67 FR 20370 (Apr. 24, 2002); 67 FR 62872 (Oct. 9, 2002). Corroborated by NRC ML043420461 and ML14294A370.

=== THE TWO LIMITS ASKED FOR ===

1) ANNUAL LIMIT — 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(1):
   The total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) to individual members of the public from the licensed operation must not exceed 0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year.
   Excluded from that dose: background radiation; any medical administration the individual has received; exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under 10 CFR 35.75; voluntary participation in medical research programs; and the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage under 10 CFR 20.2003.

2) HOURLY LIMIT IN AN UNRESTRICTED AREA — 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(2):
   The dose in any unrestricted area from external sources must not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv = 20 microSv) in any one hour, exclusive of dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released under 10 CFR 35.75.

Quantity distinction (important, and often the source of error): the annual limit is a TEDE limit covering all pathways from the licensed operation (external plus inhalation/ingestion of effluents); the one-hour limit is expressly limited to dose from EXTERNAL SOURCES in an unrestricted area. There is no one-hour limit on internal (effluent) dose — internal dose is controlled through the annual TEDE and through the Appendix B Table 2 effluent concentration limits used in the 20.1302(b)(2) compliance path.

=== ADJACENT PROVISIONS A PRACTITIONER MUST NOT CONFUSE WITH THE LIMITS ===

- 20.1301(b): if the licensee permits members of the public access to controlled areas, the public limits still apply to those individuals.
- 20.1301(c): visitor exception — a licensee may permit a visitor of an individual who cannot be released under 35.75 to receive more than 0.1 rem, provided the dose does not exceed 0.5 rem (5 mSv) and the authorized user determines beforehand that the visit is appropriate. This is a narrow medical-related exception, not a public limit.
- 20.1301(d): a licensee or applicant may apply for prior NRC authorization to operate up to 0.5 rem (5 mSv) per year for an individual member of the public, with a demonstration of need and duration, a dose assessment/control program, and ALARA procedures.
- 20.1301(e): licensees subject to EPA's generally applicable environmental radiation standards in 40 CFR Part 190 (e.g., uranium fuel cycle) must also comply with those standards.
- 20.1301(f): the Commission may impose additional restrictions on unrestricted-area radiation levels or effluent quantities to restrict collective dose.
- 20.1302(b)(2)(ii) COMPLIANCE OPTION (a screening path, not a second limit): a licensee may show compliance with the annual limit by demonstrating that effluent concentrations at the unrestricted-area boundary do not exceed Appendix B Table 2 values AND that, if an individual were continuously present in an unrestricted area, external-source dose would not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in an hour and 0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) in a year. Note 0.05 rem/y sits below the 0.1 rem/y TEDE limit and is used only as the external-dose screen under that alternative; the hourly figure is identical to the 20.1301(a)(2) limit.

=== COMPLIANCE DEMONSTRATION (context, 10 CFR 20.1302) ===
20.1302(a) requires surveys of radiation levels in unrestricted and controlled areas and monitoring of radioactive materials in effluents to demonstrate compliance with 20.1301. 20.1302(b)(1) allows compliance to be shown by measurement or calculation that the TEDE to the individual likely to receive the highest dose from the licensed operation does not exceed the annual limit; 20.1302(b)(2) is the effluent-concentration-plus-external-dose screening alternative described above.

=== DEFINITIONS THAT BOUND THE ANSWER ===
- 'Unrestricted area' (10 CFR 20.1003): an area, access to which is neither controlled by the licensee for purposes of protection of individuals from exposure to radiation and radioactive materials, nor used as a residence. The one-hour limit applies to dose in such areas from external sources.
- 'Total effective dose equivalent' (TEDE) = deep-dose equivalent (external) + committed effective dose equivalent (internal). The annual public limit is expressed in TEDE; it is not a shallow-dose or lens-of-eye limit.
- 'Member of the public' — for compliance purposes the receptor is the individual likely to receive the highest dose from the licensed operation (the maximally exposed individual), per 20.1302(b)(1).

=== SCOPE / CAVEATS ===
- These are NRC limits for Part 20 licensees (byproduct, source, special nuclear material). Agreement-state programs adopt compatible limits but may differ in detail; DOE facilities operate under 10 CFR 835/DOE Order 458.1 rather than Part 20. Spent-fuel ISFSI dose limits (10 CFR 72.104: 25 mrem whole body, 75 mrem thyroid, 25 mrem any other organ) and EPA 40 CFR 190 (25 mrem whole body, 75 mrem thyroid, 25 mrem any other organ) are separate regimes that can be more restrictive; they do not change the Part 20 answer.
- Numeric consistency verified: 0.1 rem = 1 mSv; 0.002 rem = 0.02 mSv; the 0.05 rem/y external screen and the 0.5 rem exceptions are stated as such and do not contradict the 0.1 rem annual limit or the 0.002 rem/h limit.

=== ANSWER IN ONE LINE ===
0.1 rem (1 mSv) total effective dose equivalent per year to individual members of the public from the licensed operation (10 CFR 20.1301(a)(1)); and 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in any one hour in an unrestricted area from external sources (10 CFR 20.1301(a)(2)).
